**Sub-item 1 — Accesses all elements in historyList and mathList (no bounds errors)**

Judge this item on the *declared* loop bounds and indices only, not on how much of the lists the code actually traverses at runtime. Award the point whenever both lists are iterated with correct bounds/indices and a correctly-formed access to each list's elements appears somewhere inside the corresponding loop body. The access need not be unconditional or on every path: a `get(i)` that sits inside an `if` block, or inside a short-circuited expression (e.g., `if (x) { ... mathList.get(j) ... }`), counts as accessing the elements, since the presence of a correctly-indexed access in the body satisfies the item. Likewise, control flow that cuts iteration short does not matter — a `break` out of an inner loop after a match, a `return` from inside the loop, or a flag-controlled `while` that stops early all fall under the stated exception "return early, as long as bounds and indices would otherwise support accessing all elements," which is read to cover any early termination. An enhanced for loop over each list earns the point even if the loop variable is never used in the body or the accessed value is never used.

Deduct only when the code's bounds or indices themselves are wrong or absent: an indexed loop with correct bounds that contains no element access at all in its body, access to only one of the two lists, incorrect access of `historyList` or `mathList` elements (including out-of-range or mismatched indices), or array syntax `[ ]` used on an ArrayList.

# Grading Note — Sub-item 2: Calls `getStudentID` and `getAbsences` on an element from one of the lists

Award the point if, anywhere in the response's executable source, both `getStudentID` and `getAbsences` are invoked at least once each on a `CourseRecord` element drawn from `historyList` or `mathList`. Reachability is irrelevant: a call inside a loop that can never iterate, code following an unconditional return, or a branch that is never taken still counts — presence of the correct call on a `CourseRecord` element is sufficient. Likewise, the manner of accessing the element does not matter here; array syntax (`[ ]`) on an `ArrayList` and bounds errors are explicitly tolerated by this item.

Treat the call as made whenever the intent is unmistakable and the receiver is a `CourseRecord` element: minor name-case or spelling slips, a stray extra argument, or near-miss syntax all still count as calling `getStudentID` / `getAbsences`.

Apply the "incorrect call" standard per-call, not globally. Once the response contains at least one correct call to `getStudentID` and at least one correct call to `getAbsences` on a `CourseRecord` element from `historyList` or `mathList`, additional stray or malformed invocations elsewhere — in dead code, an unused helper method, a commented-out attempt, or a second redundant loop — do not by themselves cost the point.

Deduct only when a method is applied to a non-`CourseRecord` receiver (e.g., called on the list itself, on a `String`, or on an index/int) with no correct qualifying call elsewhere, or when one of the two methods is never invoked at all.

**Sub-item 3 grading note.** Award the point only when the response compares the absence counts of an element from one list against an element from the other list using a strict greater-than test oriented in the direction the problem requires — i.e., it checks that the history record's absences exceed the math record's absences (e.g., `historyRecord.getAbsences() > mathRecord.getAbsences()`). The point is still earned even if the response accesses a `CourseRecord` object or an `ArrayList` incorrectly, calls `getAbsences` incorrectly, or compares elements that may have different student IDs; those faults belong to other sub-items and do not affect this one.

Deduct if the condition's logic is wrong in any of the following ways: the comparison is oriented in the direction opposite to what the task requires (e.g., testing `mathRecord.getAbsences() > historyRecord.getAbsences()` when the task is to count students with more history absences than math absences) — this is "incorrect logic for the condition," in the same family as using `>=` instead of `>`, and the point is lost; the response uses `>=` in place of `>`; the response compares absences with `==` or `!=`; or the response never calls the absences method at all.

**Sub-item 4 — Initializes count and increments it within a conditional statement (in the context of a loop)**

Judge this item purely structurally. Award the point when the response declares/initializes a counter variable before the loop (initializing it to a wrong value is still fine, as long as it is initialized and not reset inside the loop) and the increment statement lexically appears inside the body of *some* `if` (including `else`, `else if`, or a `switch` case) that is itself inside a loop. It does not matter *which* `if` encloses the increment: an increment sitting inside only an outer student-ID-match `if`, with the absence-comparison `if` sitting beside it rather than around it, still earns the point, because the increment statement is contained in a conditional statement. It also does not matter whether the guarding condition is logically correct for this problem — a reversed comparison, a wrong matching strategy, or a condition that does not implement the specified rule at all still counts as "within a conditional statement." Errors in calling or failing to call `getStudentID`/`getAbsences`, failure to identify all the necessary students, and returning early are all irrelevant here.

Deduct if the count is never initialized, or is reset inside a loop, or if the increment is not physically inside the body of an `if`/`else`/`else if`/`switch` case within a loop. In particular, deduct for an unconditional increment, and deduct for guard-and-continue patterns (e.g. `if (...) continue;` followed by a bare `count++`), ternary-expression counting (e.g. `count += cond ? 1 : 0`), or boolean short-circuit tricks, since in those cases the increment statement itself is not contained in a conditional statement.
